senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being holy in the sense of superior moral qualities and possessing certain essentially divine qualities in contrast with what is human
pertaining to being dedicated or consecrated to the service of God
senses.comment: In some languages it is essential to distinguish between ἅγιος and ὅσιος when these refer to God (see 88.24) and when they refer to persons or objects which have been consecrated to the service of God. It is both theoretically and practically advantageous to make a significant distinction in meaning on the basis of these contextual differences which occur in the Greek NT. It is not difficult to translate ἅγιος and ὅσιος by expressions meaning ‘dedicated to God,’ ‘devout,’ ‘pious,’ etc., but it may be extremely difficult to translate ἅγιος and ὅσιος when applied to God. In some languages one can only use an expression such as ‘he who is truly God’ or ‘he who is in every respect God.’

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: persons who belong to God, and as such constitute a religious entity
senses.comment: In rendering οἱ ἅγιοι it is important to avoid an expression which means ‘sanctified,’ for the focus is not upon a particular state of holiness, but upon a special relationship with God. Those who are spoken of as οἱ ἅγιοι may also be admonished to become sanctified.|In a number of respects, οἱ ἅγιοι is similar in meaning to λαός[b] 'people of God' (11.12) and to ἀδελφός[b] 'fellow believer' (11.23).

senses.def: (derivative of ἅγιος[a], 'holy', 88.24) the movable tabernacle or the temple in Jerusalem as a consecrated place
senses.comment: ἅγιος[d] and ἅγιος[e] should be translated in essentially the same way as ναός[a] (7.15).

senses.def: (derivative of ἅγιος[a], 'holy', 88.24) the movable tabernacle or the temple in Jerusalem as a consecrated place
senses.comment: ἅγιος[d] and ἅγιος[e] should be translated in essentially the same way as ναός[a] (7.15).

senses.def: the interior (either the outer or the inner of the two rooms) of the sanctuary of the Jerusalem Temple or of the earlier tabernacle or of a corresponding ‘spiritual holy place,’ perhaps regarded as being in heaven
senses.comment: The inner room was more specifically identified by the phrase ἅγια ἁγίων, literally ‘holy of holies’ Hebrews 9:3, a Hebrew idiom indicating superlative degree. The inner sanctuary could also be referred to as ‘within the curtain’ (τὸ ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος Hebrews 6:19). See ἅγιος[a] (88.24) and 7.18.|The outer room of the sanctuary may be referred to in some languages as simply ‘the first room of the Holy Temple’ or ‘the first holy room of the Temple.’ The holy of holies may be referred to as ‘the most holy place’ or ‘the second holy room of the Temple’ or ‘the interior holy room of the Temple.’ What is important here is the degree of holiness, not so much the actual location within the Temple. It is for this reason that for the ‘holy of holies’ many translators use ‘the most sacred place’ or ‘the very, very sacred room.’ In this type of context the term ‘sacred’ may be rendered as ‘dedicated especially to God’ or ‘consecrated to God.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: duration of time, either continuous or episodic, but without limits
senses.comment: In some languages there may be problems involved in rendering ἀεί or διὰ παντός[b], since there may be a basic distinction between (a) continuous activity and (b) activity which may be defined as episodic in that it regularly recurs in related episodes. For example, in 2 Corinthians 6:10 the fact of being glad may be related specifically to the occasions of being saddened, while in Matthew 18:10 the focus of meaning is probably upon the continuous nature of the relation.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
senses.def: to not have a favorable opportunity to do something
extension from a source which is different
a thoroughfare within a city
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἀνάλυσις loosing, releasing, not occurring in the NT) to depart from life, as a euphemistic expression for death
pertaining to being impossible to understand on the basis of careful examination or investigation
to give a measured portion to someone in repayment
to take off or strip off clothing
senses.comment: ἀπεκδύομαι in Colossians 2:15 appears to be a case of figurative usage, but it may refer to the stripping away of weapons and hence the removal of authority and power.

senses.def: to cause or permit something to remain in a place and to go away (with or without implying purpose)
to depart from a point definitively, with the possible implication of abandoning or deserting
to leave it to someone to do something, with the implication of distancing oneself from the event
to continue to exist, with the implication of being a part of a larger whole

senses.subdomain: Markers for a Negative Response to Questions
senses.def: a marker of a negative response to questions, usually implying anxiety or impatience
senses.comment: In order to attempt to do some justice to the occurrence of the particle ἆρα, one may introduce a variety of terms which make a question somewhat more emphatically negative. In the case of Luke 18:8 one might translate ‘will he indeed find faith?’ In the case of Galatians 2:17 one might translate ‘how, then, could Christ ever be a servant of sin?’

senses.def: (derivative of ἀρχιερεύς[b] ‘high priest,’ 53.89) pertaining to the high priest

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ἀσωτία ‘senseless deeds,’ 88.96) pertaining to senseless, reckless behavior
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘to live recklessly’ is ‘to live without thinking’ or ‘to live without being concerned.’

senses.def: a set of circumstances favorable for a particular activity or endeavor
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be necessary to translate ἀφορμή opportunity in different ways depending upon the context. For example, in Romans 7:8 ἀφορμή may be rendered as ‘a good chance to …’ In Galatians 5:13 ἀφορμή may be rendered as ‘a good way for …,’ and in 1 Timothy 5:14 ἀφορμή may be rendered ‘as a good reason for …’

senses.def: an unwarranted reason for some event

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the part of the leg below the ankle on which a person or animal stands and moves
senses.comment: βάσις is a more technical term for the foot than is πούς.

senses.def: pertaining to being obligatorily put or placed

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: a calm or unruffled surface of a body of water
glosses: a calm (in contrast with a storm over water)
senses.comment: A calm after a storm may be referred to figuratively in some languages as ‘the water lay down’ or ‘the waves sank down again’ or ‘the water became like a table top.’

senses.def: the Aramaic name of a hill near Jerusalem where executions took place; see also 8.11
cardinal number, where there are ten instances of a countable entity
to make a solemn agreement involving reciprocal benefits and responsibilities
the verbal content of an agreement between two persons specifying reciprocal benefits and responsibilities
senses.comment: In Luke 1:72, ποιῆσαι ἔλεος μετὰ τῶν πατέρων ἡμῶν καὶ μνησθῆναι διαθήκης ἁγίας αὐτοῦ ‘(God said he) would show mercy to our ancestors and remember his sacred covenant with them,’ it is possible that διαθήκη denotes either the making of the covenant (34.43) or the verbal formulation (34.44).|In rendering the OT term brith, the Septuagint translators employed διαθήκη, literally ‘final will’ or ‘testament,’ in place of συνθήκη ‘contract,’ ‘agreement,’ since they evidently wished to emphasize the fact that the initiative for such a covenantal relationship existed with one person rather than being the result of negotiation and compromise.|In many societies, and particularly in tribal ones, a covenant is a very significant bond between persons. It may, in fact, be the most important and lasting interpersonal relationship. It is seldom entered into lightly, for in many societies a covenant binds a person for a lifetime and may even involve willingness to die for the sake of the covenantal relationship.

senses.def: (derivative of διατίθημι[a] ‘to make a will,’ 57.123) a legal document by which property is transferred by the deceased to an heir or heirs
to shine through, with special reference to dawn, and possibly implying the shining of the sun through clouds or overcast sky
senses.comment: In some languages it may be more satisfactory to say ‘until it becomes light’ or ‘until that day happens.’ This expression is generally regarded as applying to the second coming of Christ.

senses.def: pertaining to having two edges, with particular reference to a sword
cardinal number, where there are twelve instances of a countable entity
senses.comment: οἱ δώδεκα: With the article, refers to the twelve disciples

senses.def: shorthand for the twelve disciples: ‘the twelve’

senses.subdomain: Appearance as an Outward Manifestation of Form
senses.def: appearance as the form of that which is seen
senses.comment: In some languages a strictly literal translation of Matthew 28:3 might be misinterpreted to mean that there was something jagged about the outline of Jesus’ appearance. The focus, of course, is upon the brightness, and therefore it may be important to translate ‘his appearance was bright like lightning.’

senses.def: a reference to an entity regarded as relatively absent in terms of the discourse setting
a position relatively far from the speaker, writer, or viewpoint person
to carry something out of a structure or area
to lead or bring out of a structure or area
to cause the growth and production of plants
to direct one’s vision and attention to a particular object
senses.comment: In John 1:36 ἐμβλέπω may not differ significantly in meaning from βλέπω in John 1:29 (see 24.7).

senses.def: to process information by giving consideration to various aspects
senses.comment: In a number of languages the concept of thinking is closely related to terms referring to perception. For example, in some languages one may speak of thinking as ‘to see with the heart’ or ‘to look at with the liver.’

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to stand up in a manner distinct from someone else
(an idiom, literally: to raise up seed) the male role in begetting children
senses.comment: In contexts such as Matthew 22:24, Mark 12:19, and Luke 20:28 it may be important to add a note concerning levirate responsibilities, that is to say, the requirement for a younger brother to beget children by a deceased older brother’s wife and the reckoning of such an offspring as being the descendant of the older deceased brother.

senses.def: to go back toward or to some point or area (perhaps somewhat more emphatic than the series in 15.89 in view of the prepositional prefix ἐπ)
pertaining to being cursed
senses.comment: The occurrences of ἐπάρατος in John 7:49 and ἐπικατάρατος in Galatians 3:10 imply much more than being cursed by some person. In such contexts, the real meaning is that these individuals have already been condemned by God or are under the threat of such a condemnation.

senses.def: to bring an activity to a successful finish
to cause to happen, with the purpose of some end result
to set up or erect a construction, often used in connection with tents
pertaining to being the last in a series of objects or events

senses.subdomain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
senses.def: pertaining to being of the lowest status
the chief Greek deity
a marker of double alternatives
a device used for trapping, especially of animals other than birds
(figurative extension of meaning of θήρα[a] ‘trap,’ 6.24) an instrument or means for gaining control, implying an element of surprise
senses.comment: In a number of languages, it is possible to reflect something of the figurative meaning of θήρα by translating this term as a verb, for example, ‘may they be caught and trapped at their feasts’ or ‘may their feasts snare and trap them’ (see 6.24).

senses.def: a city in Phrygia
pertaining to being of the same mind or attitude
senses.comment: In a number of languages ἰσόψυχος may be rendered as ‘one who thinks the same way’ or possibly ‘one who has the same feelings about.’ In the latter instance, ‘feelings’ would be the equivalent of ‘attitude.’

senses.def: a marker of cause or reason, based on an evident fact
glosses: in view of the fact that

senses.subdomain: Up To, As Much As, To the Degree That [Marked Extent of Degree]
senses.def: in accordance with a degree as specified by the context
senses.comment: There may be a number of problems of restructuring in rendering the relationship between clauses marked by καθό[b], καθώς[a], and καθότι[b]. For example, in the case of 1 Peter 4:13 it may be necessary to translate καθὸ κοινωνεῖτε τοῖς τοῦ Χριστοῦ παθήμασιν χαίρετε as ‘how much you share Christ’s sufferings is how much you can rejoice.’

senses.def: a small piece of wood, chaff, or even straw
to signal to someone by means of part of the body, especially by means of the head or hands
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to be quite specific with regard to types of gestures or motions of the head or hands and arms. For example, in John 13:24 there is an obvious question involved, and this may require in some languages a particular signal by means of the hands or face. The same would be true in the case of Luke 1:62. In Luke 1:22 the gesture would have to be something which would explain or indicate Zechariah’s inability to speak, while in Luke 5:7 quite another gesture would no doubt be called for, since the persons involved were at quite a distance from one another.

senses.def: to ask God to bestow divine favor on, with the implication that the verbal act itself constitutes a significant benefit
senses.comment: In a number of languages the closest equivalent of ‘to bless’ is ‘to pray God on behalf of’ or ‘to ask God to do something good for.’

senses.def: a field used for the cultivation of herbs, fruits, flowers, or vegetables
to share one’s possessions, with the implication of some kind of joint participation and mutual interest
to join with others in some activity
(an idiom, literally: to share blood and flesh) to have the characteristics and nature of a human being
the power to rule or control
a deed manifesting great power, with the implication of some supernatural force
to cause something not to happen
(derivative of ληστεύω ‘to practice robbery, piracy,’ not occurring in the NT) one who robs by force and violence
a person who engages in insurrection
a place of uncertain location on the Lake of Galilee (also found in Mark 8:10, apparatus)
(derivative of ματαιολογέω ‘to engage in idle talk,’ not occurring in the NT) one who engages in empty and idle talk
pertaining to a quantity that fills a space beyond expectations or appropriateness
a degree of completeness, with the implication of abundance
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to speak of a person being ‘full of’ some quality or ‘full of’ some type of activity. Accordingly, one must often restructure the semantic relationships so as to indicate that one is ‘completely’ of a certain nature or ‘entirely’ engaged in some activity. In fact, in some languages this may be expressed negatively in the case of Matthew 23:28 as ‘within there is nothing but hypocrisy and lawlessness.’ In the case of James 3:17 one can often express the meaning in terms of habitual activity, for example, ‘always merciful and doing good things.’

senses.def: pertaining to being extensively engaged in some activity or attitude
to mix or mingle, either of liquids or solids, often involving substances which do not normally go together
senses.comment: This statement in Luke 13:1 must be understood figuratively, and it can often be best translated as ‘Pilate caused them to be killed while they were offering sacrifices to God’ or ‘Pilate ordered them to be slain while they were sacrificing.’

senses.def: a province in northwest Asia Minor
to win a victory over
senses.comment: In 1 John 5:4 ‘the world’ must be understood in terms of the value system of the world. In a number of languages the closest equivalent of ‘to be victorious over’ is ‘to defeat.’

senses.def: to be in the process of travelling, presumably for some distance
a degree of totality or completeness
senses.comment: In Matthew 5:34 ὅλως should not be interpreted as a qualifier of ὀμόσαι ‘to swear,’ for this is not a matter of ‘not swearing completely,’ but ὅλως is a degree attributive of the proposition ‘do not swear.’ In a number of languages the closest equivalent is ‘do not ever swear’ or ‘under no circumstances whatsoever make an oath.’

senses.def: pertaining to reality, with the implication of being generally known
pertaining to being straight in contrast to what is crooked
senses.comment: The context of Hebrews 12:13 is, of course, figurative.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to make straight wheel tracks for the feet) to live or behave in strict conformance to a predetermined model for behavior
(derivative of ὀφείλω[a] ‘to owe,’ 57.219) that which is owed
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ὀφείλημα in Romans 4:4 as meaning ‘obligation’ (see 71.26).

senses.def: that which one must do out of a sense of duty or as the result of commitment
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ὀφείλημα in Romans 4:4, see 57.221.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ὀφείλω[d] ‘to sin against,’ 88.298) the moral debt incurred as the result of sin
to expose oneself willingly to a danger or risk
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘risking one’s life’ is ‘exposing oneself to death’ or ‘showing that one is willing to die’ or ‘walking into the danger of dying.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to an extremely short period of time between a previous state or event and a subsequent state or event
senses.comment: In a number of contexts there is the implication of unexpectedness, but this seems to be a derivative of the context as a whole and not a part of the meaning of the lexical items.

senses.def: to travel by foot

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a person who lives close beside others and who thus by implication is a part of a so-called in-group, that is, the group with which an individual identifies both ethnically and culturally
senses.comment: It may be that of the three terms γείτων, περίοικος, and πλησίον[b], the last is somewhat broader in meaning. At least πλησίον is used in Luke 10:27 in a somewhat extended sense of ‘fellow man,’ while ἀδελφός[e] probably suggests a more intimate or close relationship.

senses.def: pertaining to being pure, with the possible implication of a quality which can be trusted
a reference to one among several objects, events, or states
interrogative references to class or kind
to carry out some activity (with possible focus upon the procedures involved)
a function, implying sustained activity and/or responsibility
senses.comment: In some languages one may express the meaning of this phrase in Romans 12:4 as ‘all these parts help in different ways’ or ‘all these parts have different work to do.’

senses.def: to learn something by surprise
senses.comment: It is possible that προλαμβάνω in Galatians 6:1 refers to actual seizing or arresting, but it seems more likely to refer to the fact that someone becomes aware of wrongdoing, and therefore the wrongdoer is surprised by being detected or discovered. It is, of course, also possible to render προλαμβάνω in Galatians 6:1 as ‘to be involved in.’ Compare Domain 90K.

senses.def: a marker of an agent relation with numerable events, with the implication of some prior or unexpected time factor
to owe something to someone in return, implying a reciprocal relationship
to be fearful as the result of being intimidated
senses.comment: The expression ‘don’t be intimidated’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘don’t let yourself be frightened’ or ‘don’t let anyone cause you to be afraid.’

senses.def: one who speaks in court as an attorney or advocate (either for the prosecution or for the defense)
a large container made of woven material, usually grass or reeds; used for carrying a variety of things, including food and produce, and for moving soil from one place to another
senses.comment: In the one context in which σαργάνη occurs (2 Corinthians 11:33), the basket was evidently rather large, since it was used to let Paul down from an opening in the wall of Damascus. It may very well have been made of braided ropes. In 2 Corinthians 11:33 the basket is called σαργάνη, while in Acts 9:25 the same basket is referred to as σπυρίς ({D:6.149).

senses.def: pertaining to being well fed on grain and hence fattened
senses.comment: In Luke 15:27 σιτευτός may, however, mean ‘valuable’ or ‘prize.’ This would simply be an extended meaning of σιτευτός in view of the resulting condition or value of a grain-fed animal. For this interpretation of σιτευτός in Luke 15:27, see 65.8.

senses.def: pertaining to being valuable or prized on the basis of its being well fed and fat (occurring in reference to a calf)
senses.comment: For another interpretation of σιτευτός in Luke 15:27, see 44.2.

senses.def: to cause a person to shake violently in convulsions

fruit tree; grows 5-8 m high; round crown and very deep roots; Ficus carica; fruit is about the size of a hen’s egg and can be green, yellow, purple, or brown depending on the type, and is sweet and soft
senses.comment: In Palestine the fig tree occurs in both wild and cultivated forms and the latter is greatly valued for its sweet, edible fruit. It normally produces two crops each year: early figs ripening in June (late spring) and late ones in August and September (early fall).|For languages in which a term for ‘fig tree’ is not known, one can often employ a borrowed term with a so-called ‘classifier,’ for example, ‘a tree called fig’ or ‘a fruit tree producing fruit called figs.’ In many tropical areas of the world there are forest trees belonging to the botanical family of fig trees, but such trees generally produce inedible fruit. It may, however, be possible for a translator to use the term for such a forest tree but with the added explanation as to the fruit- bearing quality of the trees mentioned in the Bible.

senses.def: eating together, with emphasis upon fellowship during the process
senses.comment: συναλίζομαι in Acts 1:4 is interpreted by some as being συναλίζομαι[b] to stay with (41.37) on the assumption that the occurrence in Acts 1:4 is simply an alternative spelling for συναυλίζομαι to stay with. This latter reading is supported by some manuscripts.

senses.def: to live in fellowship with others (a meaning of συναλίζομαι in view of its being regarded as a variant of συναυλίζομαι ‘to be with, to stay with,’ not occurring in the NT)
senses.comment: συναλίζομαι in the sense of ‘to be together in fellowship’ fits well in the context of Acts 1:4, but this meaning would seem to be somewhat alien to general Greek usage, and therefore συναλίζομαι is more frequently understood in the context of Acts 1:4 as meaning ‘to be eating with’ (see 23.13).

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a relatively brief period of time, implying some measure of reduction or shortening
the Aramaic name of a Christian woman in Joppa whose name was interpreted as Δορκάς (93.101)
a ruler with rank and authority lower than that of a king and one who ruled only with the approval of Roman authorities
a small opening (used in the NT only with reference to the so-called ‘eye’ of a needle)
senses.comment: The hole in a needle is variously referred to in different languages, for example, ‘the nostril of the needle,’ ‘the ear of the needle,’ ‘the mouth of the needle,’ and even ‘the anus of the needle.’

senses.def: water that falls in drops condensed from water vapor in the atmosphere
senses.comment: Though ὑετός, which means rain as a substance (for ‘the event of raining,’ see 14.10), generally occurs in contexts in which the focus is upon the ‘the event of raining,’ as supplied by a verb (for example, Acts 14:17; James 5:18; and Revelation 11:6), in Hebrews 6:7 the focus is clearly upon the substance. Though the Greek text of Hebrews 6:7 speaks literally of the ground ‘drinking the rain,’ this figurative expression can rarely be reproduced. Sometimes one can use an expression such as ‘soaks up,’ the type of term which might be employed in speaking of a sponge soaking up moisture, but in a number of instances one can only speak of ‘the rain disappearing into the earth’ or ‘the earth causing the rain to disappear into it.’|Translators may be confronted with several problems in selecting an appropriate term for ‘rain,’ since some languages make important distinctions in terms for ‘rain’ depending upon the season of the year and the quantity of rain. For example, rain falling in the dry season may be called by quite a different term from that which falls in the rainy season. Similarly, a series of distinctions may be made in terms for rain depending upon whether one is speaking of a torrential rainstorm or an average rain or a continuous mist.

senses.def: rain, whether light or torrential
senses.comment: Though most languages have a general term for rain, the event of raining is more frequently referred to by a verb rather than by a noun, since rain is something which takes place and is not regarded as a thing or mass, unless, of course, one is referring to the water which comes down as rain, that is to say, ‘rain water’ (see 2.10). In some languages the event of raining is generally expressed idiomatically as ‘God is urinating.’ This might appear unduly crude and anthropomorphic, but to the speakers of such a language the expression is often quite acceptable and has no undesirable connotations.|Though in English one may use an impersonal subject with the verb ‘to rain,’ for example, ‘it is raining,’ many languages require some kind of personal agent, for example, ‘God is raining,’ or an impersonal agent such as ‘the sky is raining’ or ‘the clouds are raining.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to give an impression of having certain purposes or motivations, while in reality having quite different ones
senses.comment: In a number of languages ὑποκρίνομαι and ὑπόκρισις are expressed in idiomatic ways, for example, ‘to have two faces,’ ‘to have two tongues,’ ‘to be two people,’ or ‘to have two hearts.’

senses.def: (derivative of φαρμακεία ‘to practice magic, to engage in sorcery,’ 53.100) one who uses magic and sorcery
(derivative of φόβος[a] ‘fear,’ 25.251) to be in a state of fearing

senses.subdomain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
senses.def: to have such awe or respect for a person as to involve a measure of fear
senses.comment: In a number of languages there are serious problems involved in speaking of ‘fearing God,’ for this might imply merely ‘to be scared of God’ as though God were some kind of bogeyman. If there is a term with the meaning of ‘awe’ (perhaps in a phrase such as ‘to stand in awe of’), this may be an adequate equivalent. In some instances awe is expressed idiomatically as ‘to stand with one’s heart in one’s throat’ or ‘to be in someone’s presence with one’s heart beating fast.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of φοβέω[a] ‘to fear,’ 25.252) to have profound reverence and respect for deity, with the implication of awe bordering on fear
senses.comment: In Acts 13:16 the phrase οἱ φοβούμενοι τὸν θεόν, literally ‘those who fear God,’ is essentially a technical phrase to identify non-Jews who worshiped the God of the Jews. These would have been Gentiles who were ‘God fearers’ or ‘worshipers of God.’

senses.def: to cause something to move down gradually
(derivative of χρῄζω ‘to lack,’ 57.39) that which is lacking and particularly needed
that which should be or happen, with the implication of need or lack to be made up
an activity which is needed
to cause someone to eat
(a figurative extension of meaning of ψωμίζω[a] ‘to feed, to give to eat,’ 23.5) to give away or dole out, with the probable implication of bit by bit
